summary: Defines a security precondition for the SDP precondition framework. It lets a session wait until security for a media stream has been successfully negotiated. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Don't start the call until the privacy lock is in place.

questions: delay call until media security is ready
what is an sdp security precondition
what does the sec precondition do in sip
how to avoid media clipping with srtp
subtitle: A way to hold off ringing the phone until both sides know how to decrypt each other's media.

tldr.problem: When media security is negotiated, the offerer must receive the answer before it receives media from the answerer, or it cannot decrypt the first packets and they are clipped.
tldr.mechanism: A new precondition type, sec, is added to the SDP precondition framework. Session establishment waits until the cryptographic parameters (cipher, key and so on) are known to be negotiated in the required directions.
tldr.outcome: Alerting of the called party and exchange of the secured media are held back until the precondition is met. It does not guarantee the stream is secure, only that the receiver can process it.

today: RFC 5027 is a Proposed Standard from October 2007 that updates RFC 3312, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated itself. IANA registered the sec precondition type, with this document as the reference.

sections.title: Why Security Needs a Precondition
sections.content:
A precondition, as defined in RFC 3312 and updated by RFC 4032, is a condition that must be satisfied for a media stream before session establishment or modification proceeds. RFC 3312 already defines a Quality-of-Service precondition that makes sure network resources are available before a call alerts.

Media can be sent in cleartext or with security such as confidentiality or message integrity. When security is negotiated, for example with SDP Security Descriptions (RFC 4568), both the offerer and the answerer need the cryptographic parameters. The offerer may offer several choices, and the answerer's parameters may differ from the offerer's, for example the key in each direction.

To avoid media clipping, the offerer needs the answer before it receives any media packets from the answerer. A security precondition ensures this.
sections.eli5: If you start talking in code before your friend has the code book, the first words are lost. A security precondition makes you wait until the code book is ready.

sections.title: What the Security Precondition Means
sections.content:
The semantics are that the relevant cryptographic parameters (cipher, key and so on) for a secure media stream are known to have been negotiated in the required directions. If the precondition is used with a non-secure stream, it is satisfied by definition. A secure media stream is any stream that uses a security service, whatever the cryptographic strength. SRTP with the NULL encryption algorithm and no integrity counts as secure, while plain RTP does not.

The precondition type is the string sec, so the grammar becomes precondition-type = "sec" / "qos" / token. It MUST be used with the end-to-end status type; segmented status is undefined.

Importantly, security preconditions do not guarantee that an established stream will be secure. They only guarantee that the recipient will be able to do any decryption and integrity checking on the packets.
sections.eli5: The rule only checks that both sides have a lock and key that match. It does not check that the lock is a good one.

sections.title: Strength Tags and Directions
sections.content:
A security precondition can have the strength tag mandatory, optional or none.

  • mandatory: session establishment or modification MUST be delayed until the precondition is met. The called party MUST NOT be alerted and the media being secured MUST NOT be exchanged. If the answerer cannot satisfy it, the offered media stream MUST be rejected as in RFC 3312.
  • optional: the answerer MUST generate its answer as soon as possible. Clipping may occur because the answerer does not know when the offerer can process media. To avoid it, the answerer MUST raise the strength to mandatory in the answer.
  • none: processing continues as usual, and the answerer MAY upgrade the strength in the answer.

A mandatory precondition in an offer needs a SIP Require header with the option tag precondition, so user agents without support reject it. That can cause the Heterogeneous Error Response Forking Problem. As a workaround, an optional precondition with the Supported header can be used.

The direction tags mean: send says the other party can correctly process the media packets I send (for SRTP this includes SRTCP), and recv says I can correctly process the media packets I receive. When media and non-media data are multiplexed, as with ICE, non-media data may be exchanged before the precondition is met.
sections.eli5: Mandatory means "do not start until we are both ready". Optional means "start now, but you can still ask to wait". None means "I know how to wait, but I am not insisting".

sections.title: Rules for Offer/Answer Exchanges
sections.content:
For SRTP keyed with SDP security descriptions, an offerer asking for the send precondition needs the answer first: it must know where to send media and which alternative cryptographic parameters were selected. The answerer cannot tell when the answer arrives, so it uses the confirm-status attribute, which makes the offerer send a new offer with the updated status. An offerer asking for recv also needs the answer, because the answer carries the keys the answerer will use for sending.

Later offer/answer exchanges that only update precondition status SHOULD reuse the same key material as the first exchange. The repeated key-mgmt or crypto lines SHOULD repeat the same data. The RFC notes this duplicated key exchange should not be treated as a replay attack, for instance by noticing that the data is identical and not passing it on to the security layer.

For re-INVITEs and UPDATEs, the rules of Section 6 of RFC 3312 apply: keep using the old session parameters until all mandatory preconditions are met. At that moment, user agents MUST start using the new parameters for media they send, and SHOULD be prepared to process received media under either the old or the new parameters for a short period.
sections.eli5: When you change the code in the middle of a call, you keep using the old code until both sides say "ready", then switch, and you still listen for the old code for a moment in case a message was still on its way.

sections.title: Worked Call Flows
sections.content:
Both examples use the same five-step SIP flow between A and B: an INVITE with SDP1, a 183 Session Progress with SDP2, a PRACK with SDP3, a 200 OK to the PRACK with SDP4, and then a 180 Ringing. The first uses SDP security descriptions (crypto attribute); the second uses MIKEY through the Key Management Extensions for SDP (key-mgmt attribute).

In the offer, A sends a=curr:sec e2e none and a=des:sec mandatory e2e sendrecv with its keying material. B's answer reports a=curr:sec e2e recv, because B can receive but A does not yet know B's parameters, and adds a=conf:sec e2e sendrecv to ask for confirmation. When A processes the answer it knows both directions, and immediately sends an updated offer with a=curr:sec e2e sendrecv. B answers with the same status, all mandatory preconditions are met, and B sends the 180 Ringing. PRACK is used instead of UPDATE because the original offer/answer is complete and the precondition is satisfied immediately.
sections.eli5: A says "here is my key, wait for me". B says "I got yours, here is mine, tell me when you have it". A says "got it". Only then does B's phone ring.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If an attacker can remove a security precondition or lower its strength, the called user may be alerted for a session with no working media, or clipping may occur. If an attacker adds a precondition or raises its strength, the result can be session failure, heterogeneous error response forking problems, or a delay nobody wanted.

Signaling integrity prevents all of these. Hop-by-hop protection such as IPsec or TLS is enough where intermediaries such as SIP proxies are trusted. Otherwise end-to-end integrity protection such as S/MIME MUST be used, and it MUST cover the SIP Supported and Require headers as well as the body.

The RFC also warns about offering secure and non-secure media as alternatives. An active attacker might inject media packets until the answer arrives, and security preconditions do not fix this: if the non-secure alternative is chosen, the precondition is satisfied by definition and media can arrive before the answer.
sections.eli5: If a sneaky person can scribble out the "wait until ready" note, the phone may ring too early or the first words may be lost. Sealing the whole message stops that.
